title: JSON in SQL Server
description: Store, validate, query, shred, produce, and index JSON documents inside SQL Server.

data.text: SQL Server added JSON support in SQL Server 2016. Until the native `json` type in SQL Server 2025, JSON is stored as `nvarchar(max)` (or `nvarchar(n)`) alongside relational columns. The engine does not store it in a parsed binary format, so validation and indexing are explicit decisions you make. That sounds limiting, but it means JSON can live in the same table, transaction, and backup as the rest of your data.

data.title: Validate at the boundary
data.text: Add `CHECK (ISJSON(column) = 1)` so invalid JSON cannot be written. `ISJSON` returns 1 for a valid object or array. Without the check, a single malformed payload will break every `OPENJSON` query that reads the column.

data.title: A table with a JSON column
data.content: The `Lines` column holds an array of order lines, while `OrderId` and `Customer` stay relational.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE dbo.Orders
(
    OrderId  INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    Customer NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    Lines    NVARCHAR(MAX) NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT CK_Orders_Lines_JSON CHECK (ISJSON(Lines) = 1)
);
GO

INSERT INTO dbo.Orders (OrderId, Customer, Lines)
VALUES
(1, N'Ada',   N'[{"sku":"KB-01","qty":1,"price":79.00},{"sku":"MS-02","qty":2,"price":25.50}]'),
(2, N'Grace', N'[{"sku":"KB-01","qty":3,"price":79.00}]');

data.text: Read a Single Value or Object

`JSON_VALUE` extracts a scalar (string, number, boolean) and returns `nvarchar(4000)`. `JSON_QUERY` extracts an object or array and returns `nvarchar(max)`. Both use a JSON path expression, where `$` is the root, `$.property` selects a property, and `$[0]` selects the first array element.

data.title: JSON_VALUE and JSON_QUERY
data.content: The scalar values are extracted directly; the array is summed by shredding it with OPENJSON in a subquery.
data.code:
SELECT
    OrderId,
    JSON_VALUE(Lines, '$[0].sku') AS first_sku,
    JSON_VALUE(Lines, '$[0].qty') AS first_qty,
    JSON_QUERY(Lines, '$')        AS whole_array,
    (
        SELECT SUM(
            CAST(JSON_VALUE(value, '$.qty') AS INT)
            * CAST(JSON_VALUE(value, '$.price') AS DECIMAL(10, 2))
        )
        FROM OPENJSON(Lines)
    ) AS order_total
FROM dbo.Orders;

data.text: `OPENJSON` turns a JSON array into a rowset. With the `WITH` clause you declare a schema, which gives you typed columns and avoids casting every value by hand. Use `CROSS APPLY` to join the shredded rows back to their parent row.

data.title: OPENJSON with an explicit schema
data.content: Each order line becomes one row with typed `sku`, `qty`, and `price` columns.
data.code:
SELECT
    o.OrderId,
    o.Customer,
    j.sku,
    j.qty,
    j.price,
    j.qty * j.price AS line_total
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(o.Lines)
WITH
(
    sku   NVARCHAR(20)  '$.sku',
    qty   INT           '$.qty',
    price DECIMAL(10, 2) '$.price'
) AS j
ORDER BY o.OrderId, j.sku;

data.title: FOR JSON PATH
data.content: `FOR JSON PATH` shapes the result set as JSON. Wrapping the array in `JSON_QUERY` keeps it as JSON instead of escaping it into a string.
data.code:
SELECT
    o.OrderId,
    o.Customer,
    JSON_QUERY(o.Lines) AS Lines
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
FOR JSON PATH, ROOT('orders');

Formats a query result as JSON

data.title: Interview angle: indexing JSON
data.text: You cannot put a normal index directly on an `nvarchar(max)` JSON column. The standard trick is a persisted computed column that calls `JSON_VALUE`, then a regular index on that column. `OPENJSON` requires database compatibility level 130 or higher, and `JSON_VALUE` silently returns NULL if the path does not exist or the value is an object/array — which is why validating with `ISJSON` and testing paths matters.

data.title: JSON in SQL Server Key Points
points: JSON is stored as nvarchar(max) with a CHECK (ISJSON(...) = 1) constraint.
JSON_VALUE extracts scalars, JSON_QUERY extracts objects and arrays.
OPENJSON with a WITH clause shreds arrays into typed rows.
FOR JSON PATH produces JSON from a query result.
Index JSON by persisting a JSON_VALUE computed column and indexing it.
JSON is best for payloads that vary by row; keep frequently filtered and joined attributes as real columns.
